Seconding a PC for games. It's more expensive up front, but cheaper in the long run. Games are cheaper, frequently on sale or even free, and you don't pay extra for online. I also think the community tends to be better, plus, mods. Real mods, not the janky limited mods Bethesda is pushing out on the consoles for Fallout 4 and Skyrim.

It's also worth pointing out that the PS4 is having a harder time getting those onto their system because Sony doesn't like letting users play inside their walled garden.

Plus, if a controller is a deciding factor because someone doesn't want to learn to use a mouse and keyboard to play, just make sure the PC has Bluetooth functionality and you can hook up a PS4 or Xbox 1 controller to it. Most games already support Xinput [Xbox 1's controller uses Xinput], and Steam supports both natively now, and you can even go into the Steam menu and set up the buttons however you want for any game, including most non-Steam titles.

You can play PC games just like you would on a console with a controller if you want. Better in fact, because you can actually customize the button layout thanks to Steam's controller interface.

You can also hook a PC up to a television. Most PCs have HDMI out, and any modern dedicated graphics card will have HDMI out. You'll want a dedicated GPU if your using the PC for gaming. A wireless keyboard and mouse help with this.

You can also get a Steam Link for about the price of a game, it costs $50. It natively connects to the Xbox 1, PS4, and Wii U pro controllers. No need for extra dongles or anything. This will let you hook a PC up to any television with an HDMI port. It will also let you run the desktop that way, not just games. So you can watch movies, browse the web, or play non-steam games that way. I use mine like this all the time.

There's also Steam Controller, which is in my opinion the best gamepad ever made.

Sony has a few nice exclusives, but PC has a lot more of them than any console. Plus, it's pretty much universally backwards compatible. I'm still running my original copy of Doom from 1993 on my current PC. Obviously not on the old 3.5 disk, but the same files transferred from one PC to the next over the years through various forms of storage.

Sometimes you do need to tweak a bit, run dosbox, or compatibility mode, but usually with very little effort you can get most any game ever released for PC to run on a modern PC. There are exceptions to this, but only a small handful of stubborn titles.
